Concept.title: {=!}Education
Concept.text: {=!}All {CHARACTERS_LINK} have the ability to educate themselves. Educations are composed of {BK_BOOKS_LINK}, {BK_LANGUAGES_LINK} and {BK_LIFESTYLES_LINK}s. Progressing in any of these will increase your Scholarship skill and allow access to its unique perks.

Concept.title: {=NvnA9WyM}Books
Concept.text: {=!}Books can be acquired from specialized booksellers found in town keeps and taverns. They do not stay in one place for long. Each book is written in a specific {BK_LANGUAGES_LINK} and is associated with a skill. Your competence in the language determines how quickly you can read it; a copy of Dictionarium Calradium lets you read any book, slowly. Books come in two kinds: Skill books grant a large amount of skill XP. Focus books grant a focus point in their skill (or extra XP if focus is already maxed).

Concept.title: {=KBsVXEtH}Languages
Concept.text: {=!}Every {CULTURES_LINK} has an associated language. Knowing a language improves your interactions with lords and populations of that culture, both in relations and cultural acceptance. Languages also let you read more {BK_BOOKS_LINK}, faster. You can learn from notables, family members, or companions whenever they are competent enough to teach. Note: Nordic is included for War Sails / Naval DLC characters.

Concept.title: {=!}Lifestyles
Concept.text: {=!}A lifestyle is a paired-skill specialization (e.g., Cataphract pairs Riding + Polearm) that unlocks 3–4 unique perks not obtainable elsewhere. Perks unlock by spending a Focus point and progressing in the lifestyle, which advances when you exercise BOTH linked skills — only the lower of the two contributes per tick. Each lifestyle also has a passive positive and negative effect that apply only while it is active; the unlocked perks are permanent. Active lifestyles include Fian, Cataphract, August, SiegeEngineer, CivilAdministrator, Caravaneer, Artisan, Outlaw, Mercenary, Kheshig, Varyag, Gladiator, Ritter, Jawwal, and Commander.

Concept.title: {=!}Decisions
Concept.text: {=!}Decisions are major actions a character can take, found in the Character tab. They range from personal (buying a book) through family-scale (assuming a culture) up to continent-scale (founding an empire). Each decision has requirements visible on hover. Irrelevant decisions (e.g., ruler-only actions when you are not a ruler) are simply hidden.

Concept.title: {=!}Religions
Concept.text: {=!}Religions are a core part of cultural identity. Each Banner Kings faith is lore-grounded where Mount and Blade lore exists, and otherwise informed by historical analogues for the represented culture. They are fantasy ideas, not statements about real-world religions.{newline}{newline}In play, most religious actions go through {BK_PREACHERS_LINK}: they perform {BK_RITES_LINK}, grant {BK_BLESSINGS_LINK} in exchange for {BK_PIETY_LINK}, and teach you about {BK_DIVINITIES_LINK}. Preachers are also notables, providing recruits like any other. To convert, see {BK_JOIN_RELIGION_LINK}.

Concept.title: {=!}Joining a Religion
Concept.text: {=!}You can join a religion in two ways: at first campaign load (a popup offers a choice), or in-game by being inducted by a {BK_PREACHERS_LINK}.{newline}{newline}Each faith has its own joining criteria, listed in Character → Religion → that religion's page. Joining a new faith zeroes your {BK_PIETY_LINK} and costs some renown.

Concept.title: {=!}Preachers
Concept.text: {=!}Preachers are religious notables found in towns and villages. They act as the player-facing interface to a faith: they perform {BK_RITES_LINK}, grant {BK_BLESSINGS_LINK}, induct converts, and explain {BK_DIVINITIES_LINK} and doctrine. They also recruit and train troops like other notables. The available preacher type depends on the settlement and the realm's contract — some faiths cannot field a preacher in hostile-stance territory. To install one in a fief you own, use Demesne Management → Religion → Appoint Preacher.

Concept.title: {=!}Divinities
Concept.text: {=!}Divinities are the gods, saints, or sacred figures of a faith. Each faith may be Monotheistic, Polytheistic, Henotheistic, or Dualistic, with a corresponding set of divinities, taboos, holy days, and forbidden marriages. Praying to or honoring a divinity through {BK_RITES_LINK} grants {BK_PIETY_LINK} and may unlock unique blessings tied to that figure.

Concept.title: {=!}Rites
Concept.text: {=!}Rites are ritual actions tied to a faith — funerals, sacrifices, holy-day observances, war oaths, marriage rites. Each rite has a piety cost, a cooldown, and a triggering condition (battle won, hero married, holy day reached, etc.). Outcomes range from troop morale boosts to permanent traits. Rites are accessed via the relevant preacher or directly through Character → Religion.

Concept.title: {=!}Blessings
Concept.text: {=!}Blessings are temporary buffs granted by a preacher in exchange for {BK_PIETY_LINK}. Effects vary by faith and divinity — combat morale, party speed, settlement loyalty, healing rate. Blessings stack with normal modifiers and expire after a set time. A faith with active doctrines may unlock additional or stronger blessings.

Concept.title: {=!}Piety
Concept.text: {=!}Piety is the religious counterpart to Influence. It is gained by prayer, observing holy days, performing {BK_RITES_LINK}, sacrificing wealth, and successful religious-justified war. It is spent on {BK_BLESSINGS_LINK}, conversions, and rite triggers. Piety is per-hero. Joining a new faith resets it to zero.

Concept.title: {=!}War Support
Concept.text: {=!}Whether a realm's nobles support a war depends on multiple factors. First, at least one valid {BK_CASUS_LINK} is required. Second, every voting noble has an opinion shaped by personality and current income — a merciless justification (e.g., mass raid) loses support among merciful lords. Third, situational factors apply regardless of opinion: distance, current wars, threat assessment. The full breakdown is in the Diplomacy tab tooltip.

Concept.title: {=!}Casus Belli
Concept.text: {=!}A Casus Belli is a justification for war. Lords expect a real reason to risk their lives in offensive wars. Justifications include cultural (Imperial Reconquest among Calradoi successors), threat-curbing, religious (faith-driven), or claim-pressing. Each Peer values these differently — a zealous lord supports religious justifications strongly. Group affiliation often signals these preferences; see {BK_IGROUPS_LINK}.

Concept.title: {=!}Interest Groups
Concept.text: {=!}An Interest Group is a political faction inside a kingdom — Peers and notables sharing a policy agenda (laws, casus belli, factions to oppose). Each group represents a share of the realm's influence (driven by member military power and population share) and offers the ruler a level of support (driven by relations, {BK_LEGITIMACY_LINK}, and group-specific factors). Ignored or hostile groups can defect, secede, or back rival claimants.

Concept.title: {=!}Legitimacy
Concept.text: {=!}Legitimacy is how lawfully a ruler is seen by vassals and populace. A legitimate rule binds a realm together. Sources of legitimacy: legal accession via {BK_KINGDOM_SUCCESSION_LINK}, shared culture and religion with the realm, sufficient {BK_GRACE_LINK}, and group-specific factors. Low legitimacy turns powerful Peers into domestic enemies.

Concept.title: {=!}Grace
Concept.text: {=!}Each {BK_COURT_LINK} carries a Grace level — a measure of how impressive the court is to outsiders. Grace is set by the court's location and its expenses. The higher you sit in the noble hierarchy, the more Grace is expected: a king's court must outshine his vassals'. Higher Grace gives political leverage and adds to ruler {BK_LEGITIMACY_LINK}.

Concept.title: {=!}Courts
Concept.text: {=!}A Court is the personnel and physical seat of governance for a clan or kingdom. Each clan has a council with positions like Marshal, Steward, Chancellor, Spymaster, and Court Physician — filling them costs influence and grants stat effects to clan parties or the realm. Kingdom-tier courts are exclusive to the ruling clan and use kingdom influence. Court location, staff, and expenses determine the court's {BK_GRACE_LINK}.

Concept.title: {=!}Innovations
Concept.text: {=!}Innovations are gradual cultural advancements (e.g., Crossbows, Stirrups). Each culture researches innovations independently based on the era it sits in (see {BK_ERAS_LINK}) and the buildings, books, and notables in its settlements. Some innovations gate item availability (e.g., crossbows in town markets) or unlock new troop options. Progress is per-culture and visible in the Cultures tab.

Concept.title: {=!}Eras
Concept.text: {=!}Eras are broad historical periods that gate which {BK_INNOVATIONS_LINK} a culture can research. Eras advance over campaign time — usually decades — and each era opens a new tranche of innovations. Cultures advance through eras at different rates depending on their education, settlements, and trade exposure.

Concept.title: {=!}Alliances
Concept.text: {=!}An alliance binds two realms to mutual defense: when one is attacked, the other is expected to join. Refusing terminates it. Alliances are formed by ruler agreement or by marriage. Ruler-pact alliances dissolve on death or change of either ruler; marriage-blood alliances persist as long as the blood tie does (e.g., a deceased ally's heir of the same clan still maintains the alliance).

Concept.title: {=!}Governments
Concept.text: {=!}A Government law defines how a realm is organized: Imperial, Feudal, Tribal, Republic, or Theocratic. Different governments accept different policies and laws — republics reject ruling-dynasty policies like Royal Guard. Governments also constrain available {BK_SUCCESSIONS_LINK}. Changing a realm's government is a Decision; vassals frequently resist due to tradition or status, so it is hard to push through.

Concept.title: {=!}Successions
Concept.text: {=!}Succession laws determine how the {BK_KINGDOM_SUCCESSION_LINK} resolves on a ruler's death. They are distinct from {BK_INHERITANCES_LINK}, which govern clans and individual titles.

Concept.title: {=!}Kingdom Succession
Concept.text: {=!}Kingdom successions are Hereditary or Elective, set by the {BK_SUCCESSIONS_LINK} law on the kingdom's de jure title (top of Demesne Hierarchy).{newline}{newline}Hereditary: no election. The succession line shown in Kingdom → Demesne is final; on ruler death, the listed Heir takes the throne.{newline}{newline}Elective: the listed line is a competence prediction. At election time, every voting Peer also weighs religion, culture, relationship, and political agreement against each candidate. The winner inherits the realm's de jure title — and if they were not previously their clan's heir, they now lead both the clan and the realm.

Concept.title: {=!}Inheritances
Concept.text: {=!}Inheritance laws decide which clan member becomes leader on the current leader's death (sovereign titles use {BK_SUCCESSIONS_LINK} instead). Inheritance defines the ranking criterion (age, seniority, etc.); {BK_GENDERS_LINK} narrows by gender. The most common pairing is Primogeniture + Agnatic — 'eldest male first'.

Concept.title: {=!}Gender Laws
Concept.text: {=!}Gender laws set which gender is preferred for inheritance, knighthood, and rulership. They are preferences, not exclusions — Agnatic favors males, but a clan's last surviving member inherits regardless of gender. Variants are Agnatic (male-only), Cognatic (eldest regardless), Agnatic-Cognatic (male-preferred), and Enatic (female-only).

Concept.title: {=!}Knights
Concept.text: {=!}Knights are property-owning nobles fighting for their house in retinues. Though usually unrelated by blood to their lord, they are part of the household — valid heirs of last resort. Knighthood is the Knight-Service: oath of loyalty in exchange for a fee. Apart from close relatives, knighthood is required to raise a new military party.{newline}{newline}The fee is property — either {BK_ESTATES_LINK} or {BK_LORDSHIPS_LINK} (the {BK_TITLES_LINK} attached to {VILLAGES_LINK}).{newline}{newline}Estate-knights remain partly on your payroll; their estate offsets some expenses.{newline}{newline}Lordship-knights are off-payroll entirely and administer the village themselves, building constructions. Grant your most productive properties — their party size scales with their income.{newline}{newline}Granting knighthood needs at least Lesser {BK_PEERAGE_LINK} (granted on joining a kingdom), the fee property, an upfront payment, and influence. Choose wisely. Initiate via dialogue with the candidate.

Concept.title: {=!}Trade Pacts
Concept.text: {=!}A Trade Pact is a bilateral diplomatic agreement: caravans of either signatory pay no tariffs in the other's fiefs. This diverts caravan traffic between the two realms, increasing prosperity, demand satisfaction, and goods variety on both sides — at the cost of tariff revenue for individual lords. Pacts cost influence to propose (Peers dislike the loss), reduce your family influence cap while sustained, and help truces hold. They last as long as peace does.

Concept.title: {=!}Peerage
Concept.text: {=!}Peerage marks high nobility within a realm. It comes in tiers — typically Lesser (granted on joining a kingdom) and Full (granted by majority vote or on becoming a ruler). Tier gates rights: Lesser Peers cannot receive settlement awards from conquests, for example. Each clan's Peerage status is shown on its Encyclopedia page. Vanilla clans start at Full Peerage; many randomly generated {BK_GENTRY_LINK} clans hold only Lesser Peerage.

Concept.title: {=!}Gentry Clans
Concept.text: {=!}Gentry clans are the lowest tier of high nobility — AI clans spawned with Lesser {BK_PEERAGE_LINK} that own {BK_ESTATES_LINK} in villages and live there. Their income is too low to maintain a roving party day-to-day, but you can summon them via the Call Banners decision. Gentry also widen marriage options for low- and mid-status players, who would otherwise be locked out of major-clan unions by {BK_SPOUSE_LINK} differences.

Concept.title: {=!}Spouse Score
Concept.text: {=!}Spouse Score governs marriage acceptance among the high nobility. Real-world political marriages were not love matches; they were status alignments. A clan leader rejects matches where the Spouse Score gap is too wide. The score is mostly the clan's social standing — its {BK_TITLES_LINK} and properties — modified by personal merits, the leader's opinion of you, and the proposed spouses' relationship.

Concept.title: {=!}Party Supplies
Concept.text: {=!}War parties need realistic resupply to stay effective. A soldier with firewood for warmth, textiles for tents, decent food, and ample alcohol is more motivated than one without. Weapons, shields, and ammunition matter too.{newline}{newline}In Banner Kings, parties consume several supply categories. Military equipment maintains party size limit. Firewood and tools accelerate siege-camp and engine construction. Other items affect morale. Per-day consumption is shown in the wage tooltip (bottom-right) or via dialogue with your quartermaster.{newline}{newline}Quartermasters can buy supplies automatically while parked in a town — they purchase what is needed (and you can pay for) at midday wage payment. Toggle via dialogue. AI parties always auto-buy and are subject to the same supply rules.

Concept.title: {=!}Lordships
Concept.text: {=!}Lordships are {VILLAGES_LINK} bundled with their {BK_TITLES_LINK}. Their de facto control is context-based:{newline}1. The de jure title holder controls the lordship if they are in the same kingdom as the village.{newline}2. Otherwise, the bound castle/town's owner controls it.{newline}{newline}A village's faction still tracks the controlling castle/town. The de facto controller takes the lordship's full income. Because a knight can hold a lordship without being a clan leader, lordships are the cleanest path to landed knighthood — see {BK_KNIGHTS_LINK}.

Concept.title: {=!}Trade Power
Concept.text: {=!}Trade Power is how attractive a fief is to caravans. The score is dominated by realistic profit — caravan entry fees (waived by {BK_TRADE_PACT_LINK}), buy/sell margins — and by raw economic mass. Cities outweigh towns; bigger and richer outweighs smaller. Buildings like Harbors add bonus power. Net result: kingdom capitals, port cities, and prosperous metropolises concentrate trade traffic.

Concept.title: {=!}Faith Presence
Concept.text: {=!}Faith Presence measures how strongly a faith is established in a settlement — e.g., 10% means the faith can occupy up to 10% of the population (it does not mean it currently does; conversion is gradual). Notable presence boosts it heavily, especially {BK_PREACHERS_LINK}. If your faith has no preacher in a fief you own, use Demesne Management → Religion → Appoint Preacher (subject to settlement-type restrictions in the faith's rules).

Concept.title: {=5yiE49du}Estates
Concept.text: {=!}An Estate is clan-owned land inside a village. It hosts tenants (serfs and slaves), produces food and gold, and has its own inheritance line. A clan can hold multiple estates across different villages. Estates are acquired by purchase (village screen → Manage Estates), grant from a liege, inheritance, or seizure when a holder dies heirless. Income posts weekly. Estate output combines with the village's general production and is affected by climate, demesne laws, and the holder's religion.

Concept.title: {=2qXtnwSn}Titles
Concept.text: {=!}A Title is the legal ownership of land or a region. Titles are landed (tied to a fief — village, castle, town) or unlanded (Duchy, Kingdom, Empire — they preside over other titles without owning a fief directly). Each carries a {BK_DEJURE_LINK} (legal owner) and a {BK_DEFACTO_LINK} (current controller); the two may differ. The hierarchy is fixed: {BK_LORDSHIPS_LINK} → Baronies (castles) → Counties (towns) → Duchies → Kingdoms → Empires.{newline}{newline}Titles are a primary source of social status and feed into many BK systems. The standard path to acquiring one is to Claim it (1 in-game year) then Usurp it. Title actions live in the Demesne Hierarchy menu inside settlements.

Concept.title: {=!}De Jure
Concept.text: {=!}The De Jure holder is the legal owner of a {BK_TITLES_LINK} — the hero whose clan tree holds the deed, regardless of whether their kingdom currently controls the underlying fief. De jure ownership is inherited per the title's contract ({BK_INHERITANCES_LINK} + {BK_GENDERS_LINK}). When a different hero physically controls the fief ({BK_DEFACTO_LINK}), the de jure owner has standing to press a claim — this is a built-in casus belli.

Concept.title: {=!}De Facto
Concept.text: {=!}The De Facto holder is the current physical controller of a {BK_TITLES_LINK} — derived from who actually owns the underlying fief on the campaign map. A title can have a different de facto holder from its {BK_DEJURE_LINK}; that mismatch is the standard trigger for claim-based wars.

Concept.title: {=1wRI8yd9}Demesne Laws
Concept.text: {=!}{BK_DEMESNE_LINK} laws define aspects of the demesne contract — duties of lower classes, terms of {BK_ESTATES_LINK}, slave trade legality, religious tolerance, militia draft policy. Laws apply to the entire title hierarchy under the contract. They can change once per in-game year, by Peer vote or by direct decree of the demesne sovereign.

Concept.title: {=6QMDGRSt}Demesne
Concept.text: {=!}Demesne (or domain) is land or governance bound by a contract — represented by {BK_TITLES_LINK}. Every demesne ladders up to a Kingdom- or Empire-tier title tied to a {KINGDOMS_LINK} (the realm's Crown or Royal Demesne). Factions without a sovereign title can create one via the Found Kingdom decision. Landed demesne is property tied to {SETTLEMENTS_LINK} like {TOWNS_LINK}; unlanded demesne is suzerainty over lesser demesnes (e.g., owning the duchy that presides over several counties).
